name: Rome
tagline: The Eternal City, layered in empire, faith and dolce vita.
bestMonths: Mar, Apr, May, Jun, Oct and Nov
whenBlurb: Come in spring or early autumn for warm light and open piazzas; skip the searing, packed heat of July-August, when much of the city empties.

ourTake.lede: Rome rewards early mornings and long dinners; the Vatican and the Colosseum are yours only before nine or after five, so book the first slot and lunch late like a Roman. Don't try to see it all, stand in one great space, a piazza, a single church, and let it work rather than sprinting between checklists. Skip the restaurants ringing the monuments entirely; walk ten minutes into Trastevere or Monti and eat where the tables are Roman.
ourTake.comeIf: You want to walk through three thousand years of art, ruins and living street life, then eat exceptionally well every night.
ourTake.skipIf: You are chasing beaches, wilderness or a quiet resort escape with no crowds.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Bvlgari Hotel Roma
items.description: The jeweller's Roman house, a 1930s rationalist palace facing the Mausoleum of Augustus, and one of the finest hotels on earth.

items.name: Hotel Hassler Roma
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: Perched at the very top of the Spanish Steps, the grand Roman address, sixth-generation family-run.

items.name: Hotel de Russie, Rocco Forte
items.description: A historic hideaway between the Spanish Steps and Piazza del Popolo, built around a tiered secret garden.

items.name: Hotel Eden, Dorchester Collection
items.description: A Dorchester Collection grande dame above Via Veneto, with the finest rooftop view in the Eternal City.

items.name: Six Senses Rome
items.description: A wellness-led palazzo in the historic centre, travertine, an Etruscan-inspired spa and Roman baths reborn.

items.name: Orient Express La Minerva
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: The first Orient Express hotel, a 17th-century palazzo beside the Pantheon, reborn with 1930s glamour.

items.name: Rocco Forte Hotel de la Ville
items.description: At the head of the Spanish Steps, Rocco Forte's polished, contemporary counterpoint to the Hassler.

items.name: The St. Regis Rome
items.description: A gilded Beaux-Arts landmark, the first luxury hotel in Rome, restored to full-dress grandeur.

items.name: Anantara Palazzo Naiadi Rome
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A full-scale neoclassical grand hotel behind a colonnaded façade on Piazza della Repubblica.

items.name: Portrait Roma, Lungarno Collection
items.description: The Ferragamo family's rooftop townhouse above their flagship, private, stylish, all-suite.

items.name: JK Place Roma
items.area: Spanish Steps / Tridente (Via di Monte d'Oro)
items.description: A design-led townhouse near Piazza del Popolo that feels like a private Roman residence.

items.name: The First Roma Arte
items.description: A contemporary-art hotel steps from Piazza del Popolo, museum-grade works on every wall.

items.name: Hotel Vilòn
items.description: A hidden 16th-century palazzo annexe of the Borghese estate, an intimate secret in the Tridente.

items.name: Hotel Palazzo Manfredi
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World
items.description: A small palazzo built on a gladiator school, with the Colosseum filling the window.

items.name: Maalot Roma
items.description: A composer's former home turned intimate hotel, a stone's throw from the Trevi Fountain.

items.name: Singer Palace Hotel
items.area: Centro Storico (Via del Corso / Piazza Venezia)
items.description: A jewel-box palazzo with a rooftop bar over the domes, central to everything.

items.name: The Hoxton, Rome
items.description: A design-conscious, sociable base a little north of the centre, style at a gentler price.

items.name: Umiltà 36
items.description: A polished boutique house on a quiet lane between the Trevi Fountain and the Quirinale.

items.name: The Inn at the Roman Forum
items.description: A discreet townhouse hotel with its own patch of ancient ruins beneath it.

items.name: Hotel Locarno
items.description: A 1925 Art Deco original near Piazza del Popolo, atmospheric, literary, one of a kind.

items.name: The Colosseum
items.description: The largest amphitheatre ever built, where 50,000 Romans watched gladiators. Book the timed guided access to the arena floor and the underground hypogeum, or the top-tier Belvedere level, to skip the crush and stand where the emperors did. Early-morning or after-dark private tours are worth arranging.

items.name: Roman Forum & Palatine Hill
items.description: The political and religious heart of the ancient city, with the Palatine rising above it where emperors kept their palaces. Walk the Via Sacra at opening time, then climb the Palatine for a quiet, elevated view over the Forum and across to the Colosseum. A private guide turns the ruins into a coherent story for the family.

items.name: The Pantheon
items.description: The best-preserved building of ancient Rome and still the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome, with an open oculus that drops a shaft of light onto the marble floor. Free to enter but reserve a timed ticket; go at opening to have the rotunda near-empty, or during rain to watch the water fall through the eye.

items.name: St. Peter's Basilica
items.description: The largest church in Christendom, holding Michelangelo's Pietà and Bernini's soaring bronze baldachin. Climb the cupola for the finest rooftop panorama over St. Peter's Square. Dress modestly (shoulders and knees covered), and consider an early-access or scavi (necropolis) tour to the tomb of St. Peter beneath the floor.

items.name: Vatican Museums & Sistine Chapel
items.description: Miles of galleries ending in Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel ceiling and Raphael's Rooms. It receives up to 25,000 visitors a day, so a private early-entry or key-master 'doors open' tour before the public crowds is the only civilised way to see it. Books out well ahead in high season.

items.name: Galleria Borghese
items.description: Cardinal Scipione Borghese's jewel-box villa, holding Bernini's Apollo and Daphne and Rape of Proserpina and a room of Caravaggios. Entry is by strict two-hour timed slot with a capped number of visitors, so it never feels crowded; book two to three weeks ahead. Small enough to enjoy with children.

items.name: Capitoline Museums
items.description: The world's oldest public museum, set on Michelangelo's Piazza del Campidoglio. Home to the she-wolf of Rome, the original equestrian Marcus Aurelius, and the colossal fragments of Constantine. The Tabularium terrace gives a superb, less-visited overlook of the Roman Forum below.

items.name: Castel Sant'Angelo
items.description: Hadrian's cylindrical mausoleum turned papal fortress, linked to the Vatican by a secret escape corridor. Spiral up through the ramps to the rooftop terrace for a 360-degree sweep over the Tiber and St. Peter's dome. The Bernini angels on the bridge outside are a photograph in themselves.

items.name: Trevi Fountain
items.description: The grandest Baroque fountain in the world, filling a whole piazza with tumbling water and sea-gods. Toss a coin over your left shoulder to ensure a return to Rome. Come very early or late at night to see it without the daytime scrum; the newly limited-access viewing area keeps numbers down.

items.name: Piazza Navona
items.description: Rome's most theatrical square, laid out on the shape of an ancient stadium, with Bernini's Fountain of the Four Rivers as its centrepiece facing Borromini's church of Sant'Agnese. An evening passeggiata here, coffee at a cafe table, and the street artists at work is the essence of the city.

items.name: Spanish Steps & Piazza di Spagna
items.description: The 135-step sweep up to the Trinità dei Monti church, flanked by the luxury flagships of Via dei Condotti (Bulgari, Valentino, the Rome maisons) at the foot. The natural start point for the city's finest shopping. Note that sitting on the steps is now fined, so pause at the Barcaccia fountain instead.

items.name: Basilica di San Clemente
items.description: Three cities in one: a 12th-century basilica atop a 4th-century church, atop a Roman house with a pagan Mithraic temple and an underground stream you can still hear running. Descending the levels is like reading Rome's history in reverse. A quiet, uncrowded marvel a few minutes from the Colosseum.

items.name: Basilica di Santa Maria Maggiore
items.description: The largest Marian basilica in Rome and one of the four papal basilicas, blazing with 5th-century gold mosaics and a coffered ceiling gilded with the first gold brought from the Americas. Far calmer than St. Peter's, and it now holds the tomb of Pope Francis.

items.name: San Luigi dei Francesi
items.description: The French national church near Piazza Navona, whose Contarelli Chapel holds three of Caravaggio's greatest canvases on the life of St. Matthew. Free to enter; bring coins to light the paintings. A ten-minute detour that rivals any museum in the city.

items.name: Basilica di San Giovanni in Laterano
items.description: The cathedral of Rome and the pope's own church, older and, in Catholic rank, higher than St. Peter's, with a monumental nave of apostle statues. Across the road the Scala Santa, said to be the stairs Christ climbed before Pilate, is still ascended on the knees by pilgrims.

items.name: Trastevere
items.description: The most atmospheric quarter, a tangle of ivy-hung lanes and small piazzas on the Tiber's far bank that still feels like the Rome of old films. Wander in the early evening, see the shimmering medieval mosaics of Santa Maria in Trastevere, and settle into a family-run trattoria. Excellent for a slow, unhurried dinner.

items.name: Monti
items.description: Rome's oldest quarter turned bohemian-chic, a five-minute walk from the Forum yet worlds calmer. Cobbled streets of independent boutiques, vintage ateliers, wine bars and quiet piazzas (Piazza della Madonna dei Monti is the local heart). The best neighbourhood for browsing and aperitivo away from the crowds.

items.name: Testaccio
items.description: The true home of Roman cooking, a working-class district built on a hill of ancient broken amphorae. Its covered market (Mercato di Testaccio) is a food-lover's morning, and the trattorias here serve the classic cucina romana. A neighbourhood for eating rather than sightseeing.

items.name: Villa Borghese Gardens
items.description: Rome's grand landscaped park, with a boating lake, the Pincio terrace overlooking Piazza del Popolo, shaded paths and pony-and-bike rentals. The green lung of the centre and ideal with children or for a multi-generation afternoon between museum visits. The Bioparco zoo sits inside for younger travellers.

items.name: Giardino degli Aranci (Orange Garden)
items.description: A serene walled garden of orange trees on the Aventine with a terrace framing one of the loveliest, and least crowded, sunset views over the domes and rooftops of Rome. Adjoining is the beautiful basilica of Santa Sabina. A romantic, restful counterpoint to the busy centre.

items.name: The Aventine Keyhole
items.description: At the Priory of the Knights of Malta, an ordinary green door hides a keyhole that frames the dome of St. Peter's perfectly down an avenue of clipped hedges, three sovereign territories in one glance. A tiny, magical secret; expect a short queue for the single peephole.

items.name: Janiculum Hill (Gianicolo)
items.description: The high ridge above Trastevere gives the widest panorama over the entire historic centre, with the domes and campaniles laid out below. A cannon is fired here at exactly noon each day, a tradition since 1847. Best reached by car or a short taxi ride; wonderful at dusk.

items.name: Galleria Doria Pamphilj
items.description: Still the private palace and collection of the Doria Pamphilj family, its gilded galleries hung floor-to-ceiling with Caravaggio, Titian and Velázquez's electric portrait of Pope Innocent X. The included audio guide, narrated by the family's own heir, is one of the most personal in Rome. Rarely crowded.

items.name: Baths of Caracalla
items.description: The towering, half-standing ruins of Rome's most opulent imperial baths, once serving thousands of bathers amid marble, pools and libraries. Vast, evocative and far quieter than the Forum. In summer the site hosts open-air opera and ballet under the walls, a spectacular private-box evening.

items.name: Appian Way (Via Appia Antica)
items.description: The 'queen of roads,' begun in 312 BC, running out of the city past tombs, ruined villas and umbrella pines on its original basalt paving. Hire bikes or arrange a private car-and-guide on a car-free Sunday to combine the countryside with the catacombs. A green escape only minutes from the centre.

items.name: Catacombs of San Callisto
items.description: Miles of underground galleries where early Christians buried their dead, including many of the first popes. Visited only by guided tour, the cool, candle-quiet tunnels are a moving contrast to the sunlit road above. San Sebastiano and Domitilla nearby offer the same on a smaller scale.

items.name: Campo de' Fiori Market
items.description: Rome's oldest open-air market fills this piazza every morning with produce, flowers, spices and stalls, under the brooding statue of the philosopher Giordano Bruno. Come before mid-morning for the real market, then watch it turn into a lively bar-lined square by night.

items.name: Mercato di Testaccio
items.description: A modern covered market that is the beating heart of Roman food culture, with greengrocers, cheesemongers and celebrated street-food counters. The place to graze, taste and understand the city's cooking; go with a private food guide for the full spread. Good vegetarian options among the stalls.

items.name: Bocca della Verità
items.description: The ancient marble 'Mouth of Truth,' said to bite off the hand of a liar, set in the portico of the pretty medieval church of Santa Maria in Cosmedin. A quick, fun photo stop, familiar from Roman Holiday, and best paired with the nearby Forum Boarium temples.

items.name: Villa Farnesina
items.description: A perfect Renaissance villa on the Trastevere bank, frescoed by Raphael with the Triumph of Galatea and the Loggia of Cupid and Psyche. Small, exquisite and gloriously uncrowded; open mostly mornings. One of Rome's most refined and least-known hours of beauty.

items.name: Ara Pacis Museum
items.description: The Altar of Augustan Peace, a masterpiece of imperial relief sculpture, housed in a luminous Richard Meier glass pavilion beside the Tiber. A cool, calm, architecturally striking museum near the Mausoleum of Augustus. Small enough to enjoy in an hour.

items.name: Centrale Montemartini
items.description: Classical Roman statues displayed against the turbines and machinery of a 1900s power station, one of the most original museum settings in Europe. An offshoot of the Capitoline collection, it is almost always empty. A rewarding detour for design-minded travellers into the Ostiense street-art district.

items.name: MAXXI – National Museum of 21st-Century Arts
items.description: Zaha Hadid's sinuous concrete building is as much the attraction as the contemporary art and architecture it holds. Rome's answer to the Guggenheim, in the smart Flaminio quarter near the Auditorium. For collectors and design lovers seeking modern Rome, not ancient.

items.name: Piazza del Popolo & Santa Maria del Popolo
items.description: A vast oval piazza crowned by an Egyptian obelisk, with twin churches and a ramp up to the Pincio terrace. The church of Santa Maria del Popolo, on its north side, holds two more searing Caravaggios and a Raphael-designed chapel, free to see. The gateway to the Tridente shopping streets.

items.name: Jewish Ghetto & Portico d'Ottavia
items.description: One of Europe's oldest Jewish quarters, a quiet warren of lanes around the Great Synagogue and the ancient Portico d'Ottavia, famous for its Roman-Jewish cooking (the fried artichoke). Atmospheric, deeply historic and central. Ideal for a reflective walk and a distinctive lunch.

items.name: Palazzo Barberini (Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Antica)
items.description: A colossal Baroque palace by Bernini and Borromini holding Raphael's La Fornarina, Caravaggio's Judith Beheading Holofernes and Holbein's Henry VIII, under Pietro da Cortona's dizzying ceiling. Grand, uncrowded and just above the Trevi Fountain. Don't miss Borromini's clever oval staircase.

items.name: Protestant Cemetery (Cimitero Acattolico)
items.description: A hushed, cypress-shaded garden cemetery beneath the ancient Pyramid of Cestius, where Keats and Shelley lie among prowling cats and mossy tombs. One of the most peaceful and poetic corners of the whole city. A quiet hour for the contemplative traveller.

items.name: Quartiere Coppedè
items.description: A tiny, fantastical district of Art Nouveau and Gothic-fairytale mansions, spiderweb archways and a whimsical fountain of frogs, built in the 1920s and known to almost no tourists. A surreal, dreamlike ten-minute wander for those who have already seen the classics.

items.name: Basilica di Santa Cecilia in Trastevere
items.description: A serene Trastevere basilica over the house of the martyr St. Cecilia, with a swooning marble statue by Maderno. Ask the nuns for access to the Cavallini fresco of the Last Judgement upstairs, a shimmering, little-seen medieval masterpiece. A tranquil retreat from the neighbourhood's bustle.

items.name: EUR District
items.description: Mussolini's monumental Rationalist city-within-a-city, dominated by the 'Square Colosseum' (Palazzo della Civiltà Italiana, now the Fendi headquarters). A striking, spacious contrast to the medieval centre for architecture and design enthusiasts, with a lake and modern museums.

items.name: Domus Aurea
items.description: Nero's buried golden palace, explored by hard-hat guided tour with a virtual-reality reconstruction that restores its lost frescoed halls. One of Rome's most exclusive underground experiences, running mostly at weekends and booking out fast. Genuinely memorable for older children and history buffs.

items.name: Tivoli – Villa d'Este & Hadrian's Villa
items.description: Two UNESCO sites an hour from Rome: Villa d'Este's terraced Renaissance garden of hundreds of fountains, and Hadrian's Villa, the vast imperial estate the emperor built as an anthology of the empire. A full day, best done with a private driver-guide to cover both without stress.

items.name: Ostia Antica
items.description: The remarkably intact ruined port-city of ancient Rome, with paved streets, an amphitheatre, mosaic-floored baths and taverns, yet a fraction of Pompeii's crowds and far closer to the city. A half-day of walking through a real Roman town; superb for families who found the Forum too abstract.

items.name: Castel Gandolfo & the Castelli Romani
items.description: The volcanic hill towns south of Rome, cooler in summer, centred on Castel Gandolfo, the papal summer palace and gardens above a crater lake, now open to the public. Combine with Frascati for its villas and crisp white wine. A relaxed, scenic day of gardens, lake views and long lunches.

items.name: Cerveteri Etruscan Necropolis (Banditaccia)
items.description: A 'city of the dead' of round, grass-topped Etruscan tombs laid out like streets and houses, older than Rome itself and utterly unlike anything in the centre. Paired with nearby Tarquinia's painted tombs, it is a fascinating, uncrowded day for those wanting the civilisation that preceded the Romans.

items.name: La Pergola
items.description: Heinz Beck's rooftop temple, the only three-star in Rome, and one of Italy's greatest dining rooms.

items.name: Il Pagliaccio
items.description: Anthony Genovese's quietly brilliant contemporary cooking, two stars held for years.

items.name: Enoteca La Torre
items.description: Domenico Stile's refined kitchen inside a Liberty-style villa on the Tiber.

items.name: Acquolina
items.description: Daniele Lippi's seafood-led cooking inside The First, precise, modern, sea-facing in spirit.

items.name: Aroma
items.description: Giuseppe Di Iorio's cooking with the Colosseum framed in the window, the most cinematic table in Rome.

items.name: Imàgo
items.description: Andrea Antonini's modern Italian atop the Hassler, the whole city spread beneath the Spanish Steps.

items.name: La Terrazza
items.description: Fine Italian cooking on the Eden's celebrated roof, arguably the best view of any Rome dining room.

items.name: Pipero Roma
items.description: Alessandro Pipero's warm, polished room, contemporary cooking rooted in Rome, and a legendary carbonara.

items.name: Il Convivio Troiani
items.description: The Troiani brothers' long-held star, refined Roman-Italian cooking with a deep cellar.

items.name: Per Me Giulio Terrinoni
items.description: Giulio Terrinoni's 'tappi' small-plate tasting, seafood-led, generous, personal.

items.name: Glass Hostaria
items.description: Cristina Bowerman's glass-fronted room in a medieval lane, Trastevere's most inventive kitchen.

items.name: Zia
items.description: A young couple's precise, produce-led bistro, one of the freshest tables in the city.

items.name: All'Oro
items.description: Riccardo Di Giacinto's playful, technical cooking, the amatriciana in tortello is a signature.

items.name: Idylio by Apreda
items.description: Francesco Apreda's spice-literate cooking near the Pantheon, an opulent, considered room.

items.name: INEO
items.description: A newly-starred grand-hotel kitchen on Piazza della Repubblica, technique with international reach.

items.name: Achilli al Parlamento
items.description: A great cellar and classical cooking beside Parliament, one of Rome's serious wine destinations.

items.name: Pulejo
items.description: Davide Puleio's intimate contemporary room, a quietly ambitious Prati star.

items.name: Orma Roma
items.description: Roy Caceres' creative kitchen, Latin-inflected, technically sharp modern cooking.

items.name: Marco Martini Restaurant
items.description: A greenhouse-like garden room and Marco Martini's inventive, Roman-rooted cooking.

items.name: Moma
items.description: A smart bistro-by-day, star-by-night off Via Veneto, refined cooking, easy warmth.

items.name: Salumeria Roscioli
credentials: 50 Top Italy 2026, No. 1 Trattoria in Italy
items.description: Part deli, part cellar, part dining counter, voted the best trattoria in all of Italy.

items.name: Armando al Pantheon
items.description: Classic Roman cooking beside the Pantheon since 1961, a family institution that never sold out.

items.name: Felice a Testaccio
items.description: The temple of Roman classics in the city's most Roman quarter, the cacio e pepe tossed at your table.

items.name: Romanè
items.description: Stefano Callegari's ode to Roman home cooking, comfort classics, done with real care.

items.name: Trattoria Pennestri
items.description: A chef-and-sommelier couple's warm modern trattoria, Lazio cooking with a wine list to match.

items.name: 53 Untitled
items.description: Two women running a tiny small-plates room, Roman roots with the occasional Asian turn.

items.name: Moi
items.description: Local, seasonal cooking in an easy neighbourhood room, quietly one of the city's best-value tables.

items.name: QuarantunoDodici
items.description: Fresh, unfussy seafood at a price the grand rooms can't touch.

items.name: Hosteria Grappolo d'Oro
items.description: A dependable, long-loved central osteria doing Roman classics without the tourist markup.

items.name: Seu Pizza Illuminati
credentials: 50 Top Pizza Italy 2025, No. 3 in Italy
items.description: Pier Daniele Seu's pizzeria, the third-best in all of Italy, and the city's most creative pies.

items.name: L'Osteria della Trippa
items.description: Roman offal-and-classics cooking with real conviction, honest and generous.

items.name: 180g Pizzeria Romana
credentials: 50 Top Pizza Italy 2025, No. 13 in Italy
items.description: Jacopo Mercuro's thin, crisp Roman pizza, proof the best pies are out in the neighbourhoods.

items.name: La Gatta Mangiona
credentials: 50 Top Pizza Italy 2025, No. 41 in Italy
items.description: A long-running Monteverde pizzeria that keeps its place among Italy's very best.

items.name: Pizzarium Bonci
credentials: 50 Top Pizza Italy 2025, recognised (Green Oven award)
items.description: Gabriele Bonci's legendary pizza al taglio counter, the slice that changed Roman pizza.

items.name: Antico Forno Roscioli
items.description: The Roscioli family bakery, pizza al taglio, supplì and pastries from a historic central forno.

items.name: Stravinskij Bar, Hotel de Russie
credentials: Inside a Forbes 5-Star, MICHELIN One-Key hotel, a bar of international standing
items.description: A drink in the Hotel de Russie's tiered secret garden, the most romantic courtyard in Rome.

items.name: Drink Kong
credentials: World's 50 Best Bars 2025 (No. 40), Best Bar in Italy on the list
World's 50 Best Bars, listed every year since 2020
items.description: Rome's globally-ranked cocktail bar, a neon-lit, Blade Runner-ish temple of serious drinks-making.

items.name: Jerry Thomas Speakeasy
credentials: World's 50 Best Bars 2025 (No. 98), a returning entry
items.description: Rome's original speakeasy, a password-and-membership 1920s den that started the city's cocktail revival.

items.name: Cielo Terrace, Hotel de la Ville
credentials: A landmark rooftop bar, atop a MICHELIN One-Key hotel
items.description: A rooftop cocktail terrace at the top of the Spanish Steps, the domes of Rome laid out below.

items.name: Il Giardino Ristorante & Terrace, Hotel Eden
credentials: Atop a Forbes 5-Star, MICHELIN One-Key hotel, a landmark rooftop
items.description: The Eden's celebrated rooftop, arguably the single best panorama of Rome over a considered drink.

items.name: Freni e Frizioni
items.description: A former mechanic's garage turned Trastevere institution, aperitivo on the terrace above the river.

plan.heading: 4 days in Rome, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Settle in at the Hotel de Russie, then the Colosseum and Palatine Hill with a private guide.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Roman Forum walked slowly, then the Pantheon in the late light.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Il Pagliaccio, two Michelin stars near the Tiber.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Vatican Museums and Sistine Chapel on a keys-and-doors early access, before the doors open.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: St Peter's Basilica and the dome, then a rest in the Borghese gardens.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at La Pergola, Heinz Beck's three stars above the city.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The Galleria Borghese, booked, for the Bernini marbles and the Caravaggios.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Piazza Navona, the Spanish Steps, and the artisans of Via dei Coronari on foot.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Roscioli or Armando al Pantheon, Roman and honest.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A car to Villa d'Este for the fountains and the terraced gardens.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Hadrian's Villa nearby, the emperor's ruins among the olives.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A last dinner at Pipero, contemporary Roman, near the hotel.

items.name: Centro Storico (near Piazza Navona / Pantheon)
items.description: The monumental heart, walkable to everything; suits a first visit despite the crowds.

items.name: Monti
items.description: Village-like, arty and full of good food, between the Forum and the station; suits repeat visitors who want character.

items.name: Trastevere
items.description: Cobbled, atmospheric and lively at night; suits those who want the classic Roman evening on the doorstep.

events.name: Natale di Roma
events.note: The city's own birthday, marked with historical re-enactments and a costumed parade through the Circus Maximus and the Fori.

events.name: Estate Romana
events.note: The summer-long festival of open-air cinema, concerts and events along the Tiber and across the city's squares.

events.name: Holy Week & Easter
events.note: Rome's most solemn season, with the papal ceremonies and the Via Crucis at the Colosseum drawing pilgrims from everywhere.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: The centro storico around Piazza di Spagna or the quiet streets near the Pantheon are the best bases; churches require covered shoulders and knees, and privileged early or after-hours access to the Vatican and major sites is worth arranging in advance.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Fiumicino; a chauffeured car makes the 40-minute run into the historic centre, with a driver who knows the restricted-traffic zones.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver plus a great deal of walking, since the centro storico is compact and much of it is closed to cars.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Good throughout; a TIM or Vodafone eSIM is easy, and hotels have reliable wifi.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Euro; cards are widely accepted, though a little cash is handy for small cafes and tips; service is often included and a few euros suffices otherwise.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: April-May and late September-October are ideal: warm, clear and walkable before and after the heat. Avoid July-August's oppressive heat and packed sites; winter is mild but wetter.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Air India resumed nonstop Delhi-Rome in March 2026, four times weekly on a Boeing 787-8 with flat-bed business; otherwise a Gulf hub (Qatar Qsuite, Emirates) connects Mumbai and Bengaluru well. On the direct 787, request a forward cabin seat and use the lounge at Fiumicino's Terminal 3 on arrival planning.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations beyond routine; safe, with normal vigilance for pickpocketing around the Colosseum, Termini and on crowded buses. Tap water, including the street nasoni fountains, is safe to drink.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Very easy for vegetarians; Italian cooking is naturally veg-friendly, though Jain and no-onion-garlic need a clear word ahead. Good Indian is limited but present; better to lean on Rome's excellent meat-free trattorias and brief kitchens rather than seek out Indian.
